disclaimer: LeafDoc gives a likely diagnosis from a photo, not a lab test. Confirm with a local agricultural extension officer before spending on chemicals. Always read and follow the product label, wear protective gear, and respect pre-harvest intervals.

classes.label: Apple___Apple_scab
classes.name: Apple scab
classes.summary: A common fungal disease that causes olive-brown, velvety spots on leaves and corky scabs on fruit.
classes.cause: The fungus overwinters in fallen infected leaves. In spring, rain splashes and wind carry spores to young leaves and fruit. Cool (13–24 °C), wet weather with leaves staying wet for 9+ hours drives infection.
symptoms: Olive-green to brown velvety spots on the upper leaf surface
Spots darken and leaves may curl, yellow and drop early
Dark, corky, cracked scabs on fruit
organic: Rake up and destroy or hot-compost fallen leaves in autumn to remove the spore source
Spray sulfur or lime-sulfur at green tip through petal fall, repeating after rain
Prune the canopy open so leaves dry faster
chemical: Protectant fungicides such as captan or mancozeb from bud break, every 7–10 days in wet spells
Systemic options such as myclobutanil or difenoconazole after infection periods; rotate groups to avoid resistance
prevention: Plant scab-resistant varieties (e.g. Liberty, Enterprise, Freedom)
Avoid overhead irrigation; water at the base in the morning
Shred leaves with a mower or apply urea to fallen leaves to speed decomposition

classes.label: Apple___Black_rot
classes.name: Apple black rot
classes.summary: A fungal disease causing purple-edged 'frog-eye' leaf spots, rotting fruit and cankers on branches.
classes.cause: The fungus lives in dead wood, cankers and mummified fruit left on the tree. Spores spread in warm, wet weather and enter through wounds, leaf tissue and fruit.
symptoms: Small purple spots that grow into brown 'frog-eye' spots with a purple margin
Fruit rot starting at the blossom end, turning black and wrinkled (mummies)
Sunken, reddish-brown cankers on limbs
organic: Remove mummified fruit and prune out dead wood and cankers, cutting 15 cm below visible damage
Burn or bin prunings — do not leave them under the tree
Copper or sulfur sprays during bloom and early fruit set can reduce infection
chemical: Captan or thiophanate-methyl from petal fall on a 10–14 day schedule
Strobilurins (e.g. trifloxystrobin) as part of a rotation
prevention: Keep trees vigorous with balanced fertiliser and watering
Avoid wounding bark; control fire blight and insects that create entry points
Remove nearby wild or abandoned apple trees that harbour the fungus

classes.label: Apple___Cedar_apple_rust
classes.name: Cedar apple rust
classes.summary: A rust fungus that alternates between junipers/cedars and apples, causing bright orange-yellow leaf spots.
classes.cause: Orange gelatinous galls on nearby juniper or red cedar release spores in wet spring weather. The spores travel on the wind (up to several km) and infect young apple leaves.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on the upper leaf surface
Small tube-like structures on the leaf underside later in summer
Early leaf drop and deformed fruit in severe cases
organic: Remove galls from nearby junipers in late winter, before they swell in spring rain
Sulfur sprays from pink bud to a few weeks after petal fall
chemical: Myclobutanil or other DMI fungicides from pink bud through early summer
Mancozeb as a protectant in wet springs
prevention: Plant rust-resistant apple varieties (e.g. Redfree, Liberty)
Do not plant junipers or red cedars near apple trees where possible

classes.label: Apple___healthy
classes.name: Healthy apple leaf

classes.cause: No pathogen detected.
symptoms: Uniform green colour
No spots, lesions or powdery growth
organic: No treatment needed
chemical: No treatment needed
prevention: Keep checking leaves weekly during wet weather
Clean up fallen leaves and fruit each autumn
Prune for airflow and avoid wetting the foliage

classes.label: Blueberry___healthy
classes.name: Healthy blueberry leaf
classes.summary: No disease detected. The leaf looks healthy.
classes.cause: No pathogen detected.
symptoms: Uniform green colour
No spots or red-ringed lesions
organic: No treatment needed
chemical: No treatment needed

Water at the base and prune old canes for airflow

classes.label: Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew
classes.name: Cherry powdery mildew
classes.summary: A fungus that coats leaves and shoots in a white powder, weakening the tree and spoiling fruit.
classes.cause: Spores overwinter in bark and buds and spread on wind. Unlike most fungi it thrives in warm, humid weather without needing rain, especially in dense canopies.
symptoms: White to grey powdery patches on young leaves, often on the underside first
Leaves curl upward, pucker and may turn brittle
Powdery growth on fruit near harvest
organic: Spray sulfur, potassium bicarbonate or a 1% horticultural oil at the first sign
Milk spray (1 part milk to 9 parts water) weekly on small trees
Remove water sprouts and heavily infected shoots
chemical: Myclobutanil, trifloxystrobin or quinoxyfen, rotating between groups
Begin at shuck fall and continue through harvest in high-risk years
prevention: Prune for an open canopy and good sun exposure
Avoid excess nitrogen, which produces soft, susceptible growth
Manage irrigation so the canopy is not constantly humid

classes.label: Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy
classes.name: Healthy cherry leaf
classes.summary: No disease detected. The leaf looks healthy.
classes.cause: No pathogen detected.
symptoms: Glossy green leaf
No powdery coating or shot-holes
organic: No treatment needed
chemical: No treatment needed
prevention: Prune in dry weather to reduce canker infections
Keep an open canopy and clean up leaf litter

classes.label: Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray_leaf_spot
classes.name: Gray leaf spot
classes.summary: A fungal disease producing long, rectangular grey-tan lesions between leaf veins; it can cut yield sharply.
classes.cause: The fungus survives in corn residue on the soil surface. Long periods of high humidity, fog or dew and warm temperatures (25–30 °C) favour spread, especially in continuous corn with no-till.
symptoms: Small tan spots with yellow halos on lower leaves
Lesions become long, narrow, rectangular and grey, bounded by veins
Lesions merge and whole leaves die from the bottom up
organic: Rotate out of corn for at least one year
Bury or break down infected residue after harvest
Remove badly affected lower leaves in small gardens
chemical: Strobilurin or triazole fungicides (e.g. azoxystrobin, pyraclostrobin, propiconazole) at tasseling if lesions are on the third leaf below the ear
Follow local thresholds — spraying is rarely economic on resistant hybrids
prevention: Grow tolerant or resistant hybrids
Improve airflow with appropriate plant spacing
Avoid planting corn after corn in fields with a history of the disease

classes.label: Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_
classes.name: Common rust
classes.summary: A rust fungus that forms small, powdery, cinnamon-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces.
classes.cause: Spores blow in on the wind from warmer regions every season. Cool nights (16–23 °C) with heavy dew and high humidity favour infection.
symptoms: Small oval to elongated brick-red to brown pustules on both sides of the leaf
Pustules rupture and release rusty powder that rubs off on fingers
Heavy infection yellows and kills leaves
organic: Remove heavily infected leaves in small plots
Sulfur dust can slow spread on sweet corn in gardens
Plant early so the crop matures before rust pressure peaks
chemical: Triazole or strobilurin fungicides (e.g. propiconazole, azoxystrobin) when pustules appear before tasseling on susceptible hybrids
prevention: Grow rust-resistant hybrids
Balanced fertilisation — avoid excess nitrogen
Scout regularly from knee-high stage

classes.label: Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight
classes.name: Northern leaf blight
classes.summary: A fungal disease with long, cigar-shaped grey-green lesions that can destroy leaf area before grain fill.
classes.cause: The fungus overwinters in infected residue. Moderate temperatures (18–27 °C) with long dew periods or rain spread spores from lower to upper leaves.
symptoms: Cigar-shaped, grey-green to tan lesions 2.5–15 cm long
Lesions start on lower leaves and move upward
Dark spore masses inside lesions in humid weather
organic: Crop rotation with non-grass crops for 1–2 years
Till or decompose infected residue
Remove infected lower leaves in home gardens
chemical: Fungicides such as azoxystrobin + propiconazole between tasseling and silking if lesions reach the ear leaf
prevention: Plant hybrids with Ht resistance genes
Avoid dense planting in humid areas
Scout from V8 stage, especially after wet weeks

classes.label: Corn_(maize)___healthy
classes.name: Healthy corn leaf
classes.summary: No disease detected. The leaf looks healthy.
classes.cause: No pathogen detected.
symptoms: Even green colour
No lesions, pustules or streaks
organic: No treatment needed
chemical: No treatment needed
prevention: Rotate crops and manage residue
Choose disease-resistant hybrids for your region

classes.label: Grape___Black_rot
classes.name: Grape black rot
classes.summary: A destructive fungal disease that spots leaves and turns berries into hard, black, shrivelled mummies.
classes.cause: The fungus overwinters in mummified berries and canes. Warm, wet spring and early summer weather releases spores that infect all young green tissue.
symptoms: Circular tan-brown leaf spots with dark borders and tiny black dots
Berries turn brown, then shrivel into hard black mummies
Black elongated lesions on shoots and tendrils
organic: Remove and destroy all mummies from vines and the ground
Prune out infected canes during dormancy
Copper or sulfur sprays from early shoot growth through bunch closure (check variety sensitivity)
chemical: Mancozeb or captan as protectants from 2–3 inch shoots
Myclobutanil or tebuconazole in the critical window from bloom to 4 weeks after
prevention: Train and prune vines for good air movement and sun
Control weeds under the trellis
Plant resistant varieties where available

classes.label: Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles)
classes.name: Esca (black measles)
classes.pathogen: Phaeomoniella and Phaeoacremonium fungi (trunk disease complex)
classes.summary: A trunk-wood disease that causes 'tiger-stripe' leaf patterns and spotted berries; vines can collapse suddenly.
classes.cause: Wood-rotting fungi enter through large pruning wounds and slowly colonise the trunk. Symptoms flare in hot summers, especially after heavy rain followed by heat.
symptoms: Interveinal yellow or red stripes that turn brown — a 'tiger-stripe' pattern
Small dark spots on berries ('measles')
Sudden wilting and death of the whole vine (apoplexy) in hot weather
organic: There is no cure. Cut out affected arms or trunks well below dark-streaked wood and retrain a new shoot
Seal large pruning wounds with a wound paste or a Trichoderma-based biological protectant
chemical: No curative chemical treatment exists
Protect fresh pruning wounds with registered wound protectants (e.g. thiophanate-methyl based products where approved)
prevention: Prune late in dormancy and in dry weather
Avoid large cuts; use double pruning on big vines
Remove and burn dead vines and prunings

classes.label: Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spot)
classes.name: Grape leaf blight (Isariopsis leaf spot)
classes.summary: A fungal leaf spot that forms angular dark-brown patches and causes early defoliation.
classes.cause: The fungus survives on fallen leaves. Warm, humid conditions and rain splash spread it, mostly late in the season on older leaves.
symptoms: Irregular dark red-brown spots on older leaves, often with a yellow edge
Spots merge into large necrotic patches
Premature leaf drop that weakens the vine
organic: Collect and destroy fallen leaves
Copper-based sprays (Bordeaux mixture) at early signs
chemical: Mancozeb, copper oxychloride or carbendazim-based sprays as per local recommendations
prevention: Improve canopy airflow by shoot thinning and leaf removal
Avoid overhead irrigation

classes.label: Grape___healthy
classes.name: Healthy grape leaf
classes.summary: No disease detected. The leaf looks healthy.
classes.cause: No pathogen detected.
symptoms: Even green colour
No spots, stripes or mildew
organic: No treatment needed
chemical: No treatment needed
prevention: Keep an open canopy and remove mummies at pruning
Watch for downy and powdery mildew after rain

classes.label: Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening)
classes.name: Citrus greening (Huanglongbing)
classes.pathogen: Candidatus Liberibacter spp. (bacterium) spread by the Asian citrus psyllid
classes.summary: An incurable bacterial disease spread by a tiny insect. It causes blotchy yellow leaves, bitter misshapen fruit and eventual tree death.
classes.cause: Bacteria live in the tree's sap and are carried tree to tree by the Asian citrus psyllid. Infected budwood also spreads it.
symptoms: Blotchy, asymmetric yellow mottling across leaf veins (unlike nutrient deficiency, which is symmetric)
Small, upright, yellow leaves and twig dieback
Small, lopsided, bitter fruit that stays green at the bottom
organic: No cure. Remove and destroy confirmed infected trees to protect neighbours
Control psyllids with neem oil, horticultural oil or insecticidal soap on new flushes
Release or protect natural enemies like Tamarixia radiata
chemical: No chemical cures the bacterium
Systemic insecticides (e.g. imidacloprid) or foliar sprays to control psyllids, following local programmes and bee safety rules
prevention: Buy certified disease-free nursery trees only
Inspect new leaf flushes for psyllids and report suspected cases to your local agriculture department
Keep trees well fed — nutrition slows decline but does not cure

classes.label: Peach___Bacterial_spot
classes.name: Peach bacterial spot
classes.summary: A bacterial disease causing angular leaf spots that fall out as 'shot-holes', plus pitted fruit.
classes.cause: Bacteria overwinter in twig cankers and spread by wind-driven rain, especially on sandy soils and in warm, windy, wet weather.
symptoms: Small angular purple-brown spots on leaves, often near the tip
Spot centres drop out leaving a shot-hole look; leaves yellow and fall
Pitted, cracked spots on fruit
organic: Copper sprays at leaf fall and before bud break (use low rates in season to avoid leaf burn)
Prune out cankered twigs in dry weather
chemical: Fixed copper in dormancy plus oxytetracycline during the season where registered
prevention: Plant tolerant varieties
Use windbreaks and avoid over-fertilising with nitrogen
Do not work in the orchard when leaves are wet

classes.label: Peach___healthy
classes.name: Healthy peach leaf
classes.summary: No disease detected. The leaf looks healthy.
classes.cause: No pathogen detected.
symptoms: Even green colour
No shot-holes, curling or spots
organic: No treatment needed
chemical: No treatment needed

Thin fruit and prune for airflow

classes.label: Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot
classes.name: Pepper bacterial spot
classes.summary: A bacterial disease that causes water-soaked leaf spots, leaf drop and scabby fruit in warm, wet weather.
classes.cause: Bacteria come in on infected seed or transplants and survive on plant debris. Rain splash, overhead watering and handling wet plants spread it.
symptoms: Small water-soaked spots that turn brown with a yellow halo
Heavy leaf yellowing and drop, exposing fruit to sunscald
Raised, scabby spots on fruit
organic: Remove and destroy infected plants or leaves
Copper-based sprays every 7–10 days in wet weather
Use hot-water treated seed (50 °C for 25 minutes)
chemical: Copper hydroxide plus mancozeb tank mix as a protectant
Acibenzolar-S-methyl (plant defence activator) where registered
prevention: Buy certified disease-free seed and transplants
Rotate away from peppers and tomatoes for 2–3 years
Drip irrigate; never work among wet plants

classes.label: Pepper,_bell___healthy
classes.name: Healthy pepper leaf
classes.summary: No disease detected. The leaf looks healthy.
classes.cause: No pathogen detected.
symptoms: Glossy, even green colour
No spots or yellowing
organic: No treatment needed
chemical: No treatment needed
prevention: Water at soil level and mulch to stop soil splash
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops

classes.label: Potato___Early_blight
classes.name: Potato early blight
classes.summary: A fungal disease with brown 'target-ring' spots on older leaves, mostly on stressed plants.
classes.cause: The fungus survives in soil and plant debris. Warm days, wet nights and plant stress (poor nutrition, drought, age) make lower leaves susceptible.
symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings like a target, usually on lower leaves first
Yellow tissue around the spots
Leaves die from the bottom of the plant up
organic: Remove infected lower leaves and keep foliage dry
Copper or Bacillus subtilis-based biofungicides every 7–10 days
Mulch to stop soil splashing onto leaves
chemical: Chlorothalonil or mancozeb as protectants
Azoxystrobin, difenoconazole or boscalid in rotation for heavy pressure
prevention: Rotate potatoes and tomatoes on a 3-year cycle
Feed adequately — nitrogen-starved plants are more susceptible
Destroy volunteer potatoes and crop debris

classes.label: Potato___Late_blight
classes.name: Potato late blight
classes.summary: A fast, devastating disease (the Irish famine blight) that can kill plants and rot tubers within days in cool, wet weather.
classes.cause: A water mould that spreads by airborne spores from infected plants, cull piles and volunteer potatoes. Cool (10–24 °C), humid or rainy weather lets it explode.
symptoms: Large, dark, water-soaked patches, often at leaf tips and edges
White fuzzy growth on the leaf underside in humid mornings
Brown, firm rot on tubers with a reddish-brown granular interior
organic: Act fast: remove and bag infected plants — do not compost
Copper sprays as a protectant before and during wet spells
Cut and remove haulms 2–3 weeks before harvest to protect tubers
chemical: Protectants such as mancozeb or chlorothalonil before infection
Systemic/translaminar options such as cymoxanil, dimethomorph, metalaxyl-M or mandipropamid; rotate modes of action
prevention: Plant certified disease-free seed potatoes and resistant varieties (e.g. Sarpo Mira)
Hill soil over tubers and space plants for airflow
Destroy cull piles and volunteer potatoes; follow local blight forecasts

classes.label: Potato___healthy
classes.name: Healthy potato leaf

classes.cause: No pathogen detected.
symptoms: Even green leaflets
No spots, rings or water-soaked patches
organic: No treatment needed
chemical: No treatment needed
prevention: Watch closely during cool, wet weather when late blight strikes
Rotate crops and use certified seed

classes.label: Raspberry___healthy

classes.label: Squash___Powdery_mildew
classes.name: Squash powdery mildew
classes.summary: A very common fungus that dusts leaves with white powder, reducing yield and fruit quality.
classes.cause: Wind-borne spores thrive in warm, dry days with humid nights. Shade and crowded plants make it worse. Rain is not required.
symptoms: White powdery spots on upper and lower leaf surfaces
Spots spread to cover leaves, which yellow, brown and die
Smaller, poorly flavoured fruit
organic: Spray potassium bicarbonate, sulfur, neem oil or diluted milk (1:9) weekly from first signs
Remove the worst affected leaves
Do not apply sulfur above 32 °C or within 2 weeks of an oil spray
chemical: Myclobutanil, trifloxystrobin or chlorothalonil, rotating fungicide groups
prevention: Grow mildew-resistant varieties
Plant in full sun with wide spacing
Avoid excess nitrogen fertiliser

classes.label: Strawberry___Leaf_scorch
classes.name: Strawberry leaf scorch
classes.summary: A fungal disease that covers leaves with small purple spots until the leaf looks burnt.
classes.cause: The fungus overwinters on infected leaves and spreads by splashing water in warm, wet weather.
symptoms: Many small, irregular dark purple spots on the upper leaf surface
Spots have no pale centre (unlike leaf spot)
Leaves dry and curl as if scorched
organic: Remove and destroy infected leaves after harvest (renovation)
Copper-based fungicide sprays in early spring
chemical: Captan or myclobutanil from early leaf growth through harvest, per label
prevention: Plant certified disease-free runners and resistant varieties
Use drip irrigation and straw mulch
Renew beds every 3–4 years and keep rows narrow

classes.label: Strawberry___healthy
classes.name: Healthy strawberry leaf
classes.summary: No disease detected. The leaf looks healthy.
classes.cause: No pathogen detected.
symptoms: Even green leaflets
No purple spots or scorching
organic: No treatment needed
chemical: No treatment needed
prevention: Mulch with straw to keep fruit and leaves off the soil
Remove old leaves after harvest

classes.label: Tomato___Bacterial_spot
classes.name: Tomato bacterial spot
classes.summary: A bacterial disease that causes small dark greasy spots on leaves and scabby spots on fruit.
classes.cause: Spread via infected seed and transplants, then by rain splash, overhead watering and handling wet plants. Warm (24–30 °C), wet weather favours it.
symptoms: Small (under 3 mm) dark, greasy-looking spots, sometimes with a yellow halo
Spots merge and leaves yellow and drop
Raised, scabby brown spots on green fruit
organic: Remove infected leaves; bag and bin badly infected plants
Copper sprays every 7–10 days in wet weather
Hot-water treat saved seed (50 °C for 25 minutes)
chemical: Copper + mancozeb tank mix as a protectant
Acibenzolar-S-methyl to boost plant defences where registered
prevention: Use certified seed and healthy transplants
Rotate away from tomatoes and peppers for 2–3 years
Drip irrigation; stake plants and avoid working when foliage is wet

classes.label: Tomato___Early_blight
classes.name: Tomato early blight
classes.summary: A very common fungal disease that creates brown target-ring spots on older leaves and works its way up the plant.
classes.cause: Spores live in soil and old plant debris and splash onto lower leaves. Warm, humid weather and stressed or heavily fruiting plants are most affected.
symptoms: Brown spots with concentric rings (target pattern) and a yellow halo on lower leaves
Lower leaves yellow and drop
Dark, sunken, leathery spots at the stem end of fruit
organic: Pick off affected lower leaves and remove leaves touching the soil
Mulch to prevent soil splash
Spray copper or Bacillus subtilis/amyloliquefaciens biofungicides every 7–10 days
chemical: Chlorothalonil or mancozeb as protectants
Azoxystrobin, difenoconazole or boscalid in rotation
prevention: Rotate tomato and potato beds on a 3-year cycle
Stake and prune for airflow; water at the base in the morning
Feed regularly to avoid nutrient stress during fruiting

classes.label: Tomato___Late_blight
classes.name: Tomato late blight
classes.summary: A fast-moving, destructive disease that can wipe out plants in a week during cool, wet weather.
classes.cause: A water mould whose spores travel long distances on wind and rain from infected tomatoes and potatoes. Cool nights, mild days and long leaf wetness favour it.
symptoms: Large, irregular grey-green to brown water-soaked blotches on leaves
White fuzzy growth on leaf undersides in humid conditions
Firm, greasy brown patches on fruit; dark lesions on stems
organic: Remove and bag infected plants immediately — do not compost
Copper sprays before and during wet weather can protect healthy plants
chemical: Protectants: chlorothalonil or mancozeb
Targeted: mandipropamid, cymoxanil, dimethomorph or famoxadone, rotating modes of action
prevention: Grow resistant varieties (e.g. 'Mountain Magic', 'Defiant')
Don't grow near potatoes; destroy volunteer potatoes
Water at the base and give plants space and support

classes.label: Tomato___Leaf_Mold
classes.name: Tomato leaf mould
classes.summary: A fungal disease of humid greenhouses and tunnels: yellow patches on top, olive-grey mould underneath.
classes.cause: Spores survive on debris and greenhouse structures. Relative humidity above 85% and poor ventilation drive infection.
symptoms: Pale green to yellow patches on the upper leaf surface
Olive-green to grey-purple velvety mould on the underside
Leaves curl, wither and drop
organic: Ventilate: open vents and doors, use fans, and space plants
Remove infected lower leaves
Copper or Bacillus-based biofungicides
chemical: Chlorothalonil, mancozeb or difenoconazole per label
prevention: Keep greenhouse humidity below 85% and avoid wetting leaves
Grow resistant varieties
Clean and disinfect greenhouse structures between crops

classes.label: Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot
classes.name: Septoria leaf spot
classes.summary: A fungal disease with many small round spots with grey centres and dark edges, mostly on lower leaves.
classes.cause: The fungus survives on tomato debris and related weeds. Splashing water spreads spores in warm, wet weather.
symptoms: Numerous small (1–3 mm) round spots with grey-white centres and dark brown margins
Tiny black dots (fruiting bodies) in spot centres
Lower leaves yellow and drop; fruit is usually not affected
organic: Remove infected lower leaves promptly
Mulch and water at the base
Copper or Bacillus subtilis sprays every 7–10 days in wet weather
chemical: Chlorothalonil or mancozeb as protectants; azoxystrobin in rotation
prevention: Rotate for at least one year away from tomatoes
Remove nightshade weeds and all tomato debris at season end
Stake plants for airflow

classes.label: Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider_mite
classes.name: Two-spotted spider mite
classes.summary: Tiny sap-sucking mites that speckle leaves with yellow dots and spin fine webbing in hot, dry weather.
classes.cause: Mites multiply very fast in hot, dry, dusty conditions. Broad-spectrum insecticides that kill their natural predators often trigger outbreaks.
symptoms: Fine yellow-white stippling (speckles) on leaves
Fine silky webbing on the underside and between leaves
Leaves bronze, dry and drop; tiny moving dots visible with a hand lens
organic: Spray the leaf undersides with a strong jet of water every few days
Insecticidal soap, neem oil or horticultural oil, covering undersides thoroughly
Release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis) in greenhouses
chemical: Miticides such as abamectin, spiromesifen or bifenazate; rotate to avoid resistance
Avoid pyrethroids, which can make mite outbreaks worse
prevention: Keep plants well watered and reduce dust
Avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum insecticides
Check leaf undersides weekly in hot weather

classes.label: Tomato___Target_Spot
classes.name: Tomato target spot
classes.summary: A fungal disease with brown spots that develop rings, similar to early blight, affecting leaves, stems and fruit.
classes.cause: Survives on crop debris and many host plants. Warm (20–28 °C), humid weather with long leaf wetness and dense canopies favour it.
symptoms: Small water-soaked spots that grow into brown lesions with faint concentric rings
Lesions often have a light-brown centre and may crack
Sunken spots on fruit; heavy leaf drop
organic: Remove lower infected leaves and improve airflow by pruning
Copper-based sprays as a protectant
chemical: Chlorothalonil, mancozeb, azoxystrobin or boscalid in rotation
prevention: Crop rotation and removal of debris
Avoid overhead irrigation and over-fertilising with nitrogen

classes.label: Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus
classes.name: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus
classes.summary: A whitefly-spread virus that curls and yellows leaves, stunts plants and stops fruit set. There is no cure.
classes.cause: The silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) picks up the virus from infected plants and spreads it as it feeds. It is not spread by seed or touch.
symptoms: Leaves curl upward and inward and are small and crumpled
Yellow leaf edges and between veins
Stunted, bushy plants with flowers that drop and little fruit
organic: No cure — pull out and bag infected plants early to protect others
Control whiteflies with yellow sticky traps, neem oil or insecticidal soap
Use fine insect netting (50-mesh) over seedlings
chemical: No chemical cures the virus
Whitefly control with registered products (e.g. spirotetramat, cyantraniliprole, pyriproxyfen), rotating groups and protecting pollinators
prevention: Plant TYLCV-resistant varieties (Ty-1/Ty-3 genes)
Raise seedlings under insect netting; use reflective mulch
Remove weeds and leave a tomato-free break between seasons

classes.label: Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus
classes.name: Tomato mosaic virus
classes.summary: A very stable virus that causes a light/dark green mosaic and distorted leaves. It spreads by touch and tools.
classes.cause: Spread mechanically on hands, tools, clothing and infected seed; it can survive for years in dried plant debris and even tobacco products.
symptoms: Light and dark green mottled (mosaic) pattern on leaves
Fern-like, narrow or distorted leaves
Stunted growth and uneven fruit ripening, sometimes with internal browning
organic: No cure — remove and bag infected plants
Wash hands with soap and disinfect tools (10% bleach or 20% skim-milk dip) between plants
Do not smoke or handle tobacco around plants
chemical: No chemical treatment controls the virus
Disinfect stakes, trays and tools before reuse
prevention: Use certified virus-free seed and resistant varieties (Tm-2² gene)
Work on healthy plants before suspect ones
Clear all plant debris at the end of the season

classes.cause: No pathogen detected.
symptoms: Even green colour
No spots, curling or mottling
organic: No treatment needed
chemical: No treatment needed

Stake plants and remove leaves touching the soil
Check the lower leaves twice a week in humid weather
